'''Elaine Diacumakos''' (August 11, 1930 – June 11, 1984) was an American cell biologist and head of the [[Cell biology|cytobiology]] laboratory at [[Rockefeller University]]. She developed the first techniques for removing and inserting material into and from cells.

== Early life and education ==
Diacumakos was born in [[Chester, Pennsylvania]] on August 11, 1930.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/06/15/obituaries/elaine-diacumakos-held-a-leading-role-in-cell-microsurgery.html|title=ELAINE DIACUMAKOS, HELD A LEADING ROLE IN CELL MICROSURGERY|last=Waggoner|first=Walter H.|access-date=2018-08-11}}</ref> She studied zoology at the [[University of Maryland, College Park]], graduating in 1951. She completed a master's degree in embryology in 1955 and her doctorate at [[New York University]] in 1958.<ref name=":0" /> She remained there as a research associate until 1964.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=Encyclopedia of world scientists|author=Oakes, Elizabeth H.|date=2007|publisher=Facts on File|isbn=9781438118826|edition=Rev.|location=New York|oclc=466364697}}</ref>

== Research ==
Diacumakos completed her postdoctoral training at [[Rockefeller University]] between 1958 and 1960.<ref name=":0" /> She worked at the [[Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center]] and [[Cornell University Medical Center]] from 1965 to 1971.<ref name=":0" /> In 1961 she joined [[Edward Tatum]], developing microneedle techniques that allowed her to transplant the nuclei of one cell to another.<ref name=":0" />

She returned to [[Rockefeller University]] as a senior researcher in 1971, working on cellular drug resistance and cell insertion techniques.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Diacumakos|first1=Elaine G.|last2=Holland|first2=Scott|last3=Pecora|first3=Pauline|date=April 1970|title=A Microsurgical Methodology for Human Cells in Vitro: Evolution and Applications*|pmc=283003|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=65|issue=4|pages=911–918|issn=0027-8424|pmid=5266161|doi=10.1073/pnas.65.4.911|bibcode=1970PNAS...65..911D|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CPTJCgAAQBAJ&q=Elaine+Diacumakos&pg=PA88|title=The Molecular Basis of Mutant Hemoglobin Dysfunction|last=Sigler|first=Paul B.|date=2017-01-31|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=9781483165219}}</ref> She made important contributions to the micromanipulation of mammalian cells.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8cT3XHxKY3sC&q=Elaine+Diacumakos&pg=PA171|title=International Review of Cytology|date=1989-05-01|publisher=Academic Press|isbn=9780080586526}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fgMjBQAAQBAJ&q=Elaine+Diacumakos&pg=PT71|title=Senescence: Dominant or Recessive in Somatic Cell Crosses?|last=Nichols|first=Warren|date=2012-12-06|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=9781468425086}}</ref> She studied the displacement of chromosomes during extraction at different mitotic stages.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=DIACUMAKOS|first1=ELAINE G.|last2=HOLLAND|first2=SCOTT|last3=PECORA|first3=PAULINE|date=July 1971|title=Chromosome Displacement in and Extraction from Human Cells at Different Mitotic Stages|journal=Nature|volume=232|issue=5305|pages=33–36|doi=10.1038/232033a0|pmid=4933170|bibcode=1971Natur.232...33D|s2cid=4222857|issn=0028-0836}}</ref> She demonstrated the precise fusion of mammalian somatic cells using microsurgery in 1972.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Diacumakos|first1=Elaine G.|last2=Tatum|first2=Edward L.|date=October 1972|title=Fusion of Mammalian Somatic Cells by Microsurgery|pmc=389683|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=69|issue=10|pages=2959–2962|issn=0027-8424|pmid=4507616|doi=10.1073/pnas.69.10.2959|bibcode=1972PNAS...69.2959D|doi-access=free}}</ref> She was made head of the [[Cytobiology]] Laboratory in 1975 after Tatum died unexpectedly.<ref name=":0" /> She was unable to raise funding for her own research.<ref name=":1" /> Her work with micropipettes became well known, and she worked with [[Dana Giulian]] on electrodes which could impale human cells without damage and measure the potential of a cytoplasm.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2kSx32Vshy0C&q=Elaine+Diacumakos&pg=PA394|title=New Scientist|date=1977-02-17|publisher=Reed Business Information}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|date=1977-01-01|title=The electrophysiological mapping of compartments within a mammalian cell|journal=The Journal of Cell Biology|volume=72|issue=1|pages=86–103|issn=0021-9525|pmc=2110992|pmid=63464|last1=Giulian|first1=D|last2=Diacumakos|first2=E. G|doi=10.1083/jcb.72.1.86}}</ref>

In 1979 she collaborated with [[William French Anderson]] to insert a functioning gene into a defective cell within a living mouse, correcting a genetic defect.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/magazine/1991/01/20/french-andersons-genetic-destiny/8d7bdf6f-254a-410c-8383-614a8c00f332/|title=FRENCH ANDERSON'S GENETIC DESTINY|last=Thompson|first=Larry|date=1991-01-20|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=2018-08-11|issn=0190-8286}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|date=1979-10-15|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|volume=57|issue=42|pages=6|doi=10.1021/cen-v057n042.p006|issn=0009-2347|title=Genes Injected into Deficient Cells}}</ref> Her microsurgical techniques opened new paths to curing medical conditions.<ref name=":2" /> They conducted their first ever experiment on a human 11 years later.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{cite journal|jstor=e24964476|title=Vol. 245, No. 1, July 1981 of Scientific American on JSTOR}}</ref> She lectured at the [[Pasteur Institute]] in 1981.<ref name=":0" />

Diacumakos died of a heart attack on June 11, 1984.<ref name=":0" />
